groups.title: The Document Model
groups.question: Explain how MongoDB's document model differs from tables and rows.

followUps.BSON, Documents & Collections: What breaks if you store dates and IDs as plain strings in MongoDB?
followUps.Embedding vs Referencing: How do you decide whether to embed related data or reference it from another collection?

evidence.text: BSON has real types like Date, ObjectId and Decimal128 that JSON lacks.
Dates stored as strings sort and compare as text, so date range queries break.
IDs stored as strings don't match ObjectId references and lookups fail.

notEnough: Only naming the terms (BSON, ObjectId) without explaining how they work or why they matter.

misconceptions.text: Says strings work exactly like native dates and ObjectIds.

evidence.text: Embed data that is read together with the parent and stays bounded.
Reference data that grows without limit, is shared, or is updated on its own.
Unbounded embedded arrays hit the 16MB document limit and slow everything.

notEnough: Only naming the terms (embedding, referencing) without explaining how they work or why they matter.

misconceptions.text: Says data should always be embedded in MongoDB.

groups.title: The Aggregation Pipeline
groups.question: Walk through how the aggregation pipeline processes data and how you keep it fast.

followUps.Aggregation Pipeline Stages: Why does the order of stages matter so much for performance?
followUps.$lookup — Joins in MongoDB: When does $lookup become a performance problem, and what would you do instead?

evidence.text: Stages run in sequence, each working on the previous stage's output.
$match (and $sort) early can use indexes and shrink the data before expensive stages.
Filtering after $group means the whole collection is grouped first.

notEnough: Only naming the terms ($match, $group) without explaining how they work or why they matter.

misconceptions.text: Says MongoDB reorders all stages so order never matters.

evidence.text: $lookup joins documents from another collection for each input document.
Without an index on the joined field, every lookup scans the other collection.
If you join constantly, embed or duplicate the needed fields instead.

notEnough: Only naming the terms ($lookup) without explaining how they work or why they matter.

misconceptions.text: Says $lookup is as cheap as an embedded read.

groups.title: Indexes & Schema Patterns in MongoDB
groups.question: Explain how you design indexes and documents for a MongoDB collection that grows large.

followUps.MongoDB Indexes — Types & Tradeoffs: What happens to index size and write speed when you index a large array field?
followUps.Schema Design Patterns (Bucket, Outlier): Pick the Bucket or Outlier pattern and describe the problem it solves.

evidence.text: Indexing an array creates one index entry per element.
Large arrays make the index huge.
Every write has to update all those entries, so writes slow down.

notEnough: Only naming the terms (multikey index) without explaining how they work or why they matter.

misconceptions.text: Says an array field gets a single index entry per document.

evidence.text: Names the problem: unbounded growth, like one document per reading, or a few huge outliers.
Bucket groups many readings per document (e.g. per hour); Outlier moves the overflow of rare huge documents elsewhere.

notEnough: Only naming the terms (Bucket, Outlier) without explaining how they work or why they matter.

misconceptions.text: Says these patterns only change naming.

groups.title: MongoDB Atlas & Operations
groups.question: Walk through what you need to know to run MongoDB safely in production on Atlas.

followUps.Atlas Search & Vector Search: A user saves a document and searches for it right away but can't find it. Why can that happen with Atlas Search?
followUps.Write Concern & Read Preference: How do write concern and read preference affect whether data can be lost or read stale?

evidence.text: Atlas Search keeps its own Lucene index, updated asynchronously.
So a just-saved document can be missing from search results for a short time.

notEnough: Only naming the terms (Atlas Search, Lucene) without explaining how they work or why they matter.

misconceptions.text: Says the search index updates in the same transaction as the write.

evidence.text: Write concern sets how many members must confirm a write; w:majority survives a primary failure, w:1 or w:0 can lose writes.
Read preference chooses which members serve reads.
Reading from secondaries can return stale data because they lag behind.

notEnough: Only naming the terms (write concern, read preference) without explaining how they work or why they matter.

misconceptions.text: Says secondaries are always fully up to date.
